Now let me fetch a few remaining key sources — the Desiring God article on revival, and the NET Bible notes for modern scholarship.I have gathered substantial material from the four fetched pages (Gill, Ellicott, Spurgeon, Constable) plus detailed search-result excerpts from Enduring Word, Desiring God, Ligonier, Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary, and Whedon's Commentary. Here are the verse-by-verse notes.

## Psalm 85 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

### Overview / Historical Setting

**Traditional view:** Most older commentators connect this psalm to the return from the Babylonian exile (c. 538 BC). The people are back in the land, but the bright hopes of restoration have soured — the city is ruined, enemies surround them, and there is drought or famine. The psalm moves from thanksgiving for past deliverance, through urgent prayer for present revival, to confident hope in God's coming salvation. Spurgeon, however, defends Davidic authorship, arguing that "captivity" (v. 1) need not mean exile — Job's "captivity" was turned without his leaving home (Job 42:10) — and that the psalm fits David's own era of Philistine oppression.

- Ellicott: "Its whole tone belongs to that time [post-exile] … the troubles that succeeded the return perplexed those who had come back" — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/85.htm
- Spurgeon: "It is the prayer of a patriot for his afflicted country … We believe that David wrote it" — https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps085.php
- Constable: "The reference to restoration from captivity suggests that this psalm may date to the return from Babylonian exile. However, the psalmist may have been referring to a more modest captivity" — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/psalms-85.html
- Enduring Word (Guzik): "Psalm 85 (in some ways) seems to fit the period of Israel's return from exile; in other ways it does not" — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-85/

**Messianic dimension:** All the older sources agree the psalm looks beyond its immediate historical setting to Christ. The Syriac version titles it "a prophecy concerning Christ" (Gill). Ellicott calls it "in the highest sense Messianic." The Anglican tradition chose this psalm for Christmas Day (Ellicott notes this).

---

### v. 1 — "You showed favor to Your land, O LORD; You restored Jacob from captivity."

- **"Your land":** God has a special ownership of Canaan. Though the whole earth is His, Israel is His peculiar possession (Gill). Spurgeon adds: "It is most wise to plead the Lord's union of interest with ourselves … It is our land that is devastated, but O Jehovah, it is also thy land."
- **"Restored … captivity":** The Hebrew verb *shuv* means to turn back or return. It may refer to the Babylonian return, but Gill notes it also applies spiritually to redemption from sin, Satan, and the law. Ellicott renders it "thou hast brought back" and links it to the exile.
- **Pleading past mercies:** Spurgeon: "God's past doings are prophetic of what he will do; hence the encouraging argument — 'Thou hast been favourable unto thy land,' therefore deal graciously with it again."

- Gill: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/85.htm
- Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/85.htm
- Spurgeon: https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps085.php
- Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-85/

---

### v. 2 — "You forgave the iniquity of Your people; You covered all their sin. Selah"

- **Two images for forgiveness:** The Hebrew uses two distinct terms. The first (*nasa*, "forgave"/"taken away") pictures sin as a heavy burden that God lifts off. The second (*kasah*, "covered") pictures sin as a hideous stain that God covers so it no longer offends heaven. Both terms appear in Psalm 32:1. (Maclaren, cited by Guzik; also Ellicott.)
- **"Covered … all their sin":** Spurgeon: "All of it, every spot, and wrinkle, the veil of love has covered all. Sin has been divinely put out of sight." Gill ties the covering to Christ as the antitypical mercy seat — the covering of the law and its transgressions.
- **Gill notes** that Adam Clarke saw in "forgiven" (borne/carried away) an allusion to the scapegoat ceremony.

- Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-85/
- Gill: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/85.htm
- Spurgeon: https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps085.php
- Ellicott (renders "taken away"): https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/85.htm

---

### v. 3 — "You withheld all Your fury; You turned from Your burning anger."

- **Complete removal of wrath:** Gill says God "gathered" His wrath and poured it on Christ the surety — therefore "nothing of this kind shall ever fall upon them." The satisfaction of divine anger is a key theme.
- **"Turned":** The Hebrew verb for "turn" (*shuv*) fascinates this psalmist; Ellicott's notes that it appears five times in the psalm (vv. 1, 3, 4, 6, 8). There is a constant movement of turning — God turning from anger, the people turning back to God, God turning/reviving them.
- Spurgeon: "Even when judgments had been most severe, the Lord had in mercy stayed his hand. In mid volley he had restrained his thunder."

- Gill: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/85.htm
- Spurgeon: https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps085.php
- Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-85/

---

### v. 4 — "Restore us, O God of our salvation, and put away Your displeasure toward us."

- **"Turn us" (Restore us):** The Hebrew is literally "turn us," i.e., convert us, bring us back. Spurgeon calls this "the main business" — "It is not that God needs turning from his anger so much as that we need turning from our sin; here is the hinge of the whole matter." Ellicott notes the force of the verb: "If the captivity had taught its lesson, why, on the restoration, did not complete freedom from misfortune ensue?"
- **"God of our salvation":** Gill observes that this names God as the one who appointed salvation in His purposes, contrived it in counsel, secured it in covenant, and sent His Son to effect it.
- **Baptist emphasis (Garner-Howes):** The Hebrew indicates such intense faith that the appeal is phrased as already accomplished — so faithful is God to His covenant promises. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/psalms-85.html (from search excerpt)
- **Methodist (Whedon):** "The spiritual sense of convert is implied, of which the literal restoration was a symbol … the utter inability of the nation to re-collect itself, and revive its polity, without the specific leadership of God." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/psalms-85.html (from search excerpt)

- Spurgeon: https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps085.php
- Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/85.htm
- Gill: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/85.htm

---

### v. 5 — "Will You be angry with us forever? Will You draw out Your anger to all generations?"

- **Bold pleading:** Spurgeon notes the rhetorical force: "We are in time as yet and not in eternity, and does not time come to an end, and therefore thy wrath? … Every word is an argument. Men in distress never waste words."
- **"To all generations":** Gill reads this with specific reference to the Jewish people: God's anger has been drawn out "for almost twenty centuries" but will not be drawn out to *all* generations, because "all Israel shall be saved" (Romans 11:26).
- **Pastoral note:** The question form itself implies hope — if the psalmist believed God would be angry forever, he would not ask the question.

- Spurgeon: https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps085.php
- Gill: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/85.htm

---

### v. 6 — "Will You not revive us again, that Your people may rejoice in You?"

- **"Revive us again":** This is the classic prayer for revival. Guzik (Enduring Word) calls it "a simple and wonderful prayer for revival. It recognizes that revival is not man-made, but given by God." Gill likens it to resurrection — "men are dead in trespasses and sins, and they are quickened by the Spirit and grace of God."
- **"That Your people may rejoice in You":** The aim of revival is not better circumstances but joy in God Himself. Spurgeon: "Joy in the Lord is the ripest fruit of grace … A genuine revival without joy in the Lord is as impossible as spring without flowers, or daydawn without light."
- **Reformed Baptist (Desiring God / Ray Ortlund):** "The end, or goal, of biblical revival is God's people enjoying God, rejoicing in him, having him as our joy of joys." Revival comes through God's Word — "the Spirit's flame does not land without the kindling of his word." — https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/revival-in-the-making (from search excerpt)
- **Methodist (Whedon):** Notes the "natural shrinking of the human heart from great trials discovers itself in these plaintive outcries, like 'Lord, save us: we perish' (Matthew 8:25); but faith resumes her sway (v. 8) and serenely conducts us to the close."

- Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-85/
- Spurgeon: https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps085.php
- Gill: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/85.htm
- Desiring God: https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/revival-in-the-making (search excerpt)

---

### v. 7 — "Show us Your loving devotion, O LORD, and grant us Your salvation."

- **"Loving devotion" (hesed / mercy):** The Hebrew *hesed* is God's covenant loyalty and steadfast love. Spurgeon: "Reveal it to our poor half blinded eyes. We cannot see it or believe it by reason of our long woes, but thou canst make it plain to us."
- **"Grant us Your salvation":** Spurgeon calls this comprehensive — "it reaches from the depth of their misery to the height of divine love." Gill says "salvation" here means "Jesus, the Saviour, and salvation by him, an interest in it, and the joys of it; which is all a free gift, a grant of divine favour."
- **"Show us … grant us":** Both are acts of God, not human achievement. Revival and salvation are received, not earned.

- Spurgeon: https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps085.php
- Gill: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/85.htm
- Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-85/

---

### v. 8 — "I will listen to what God the LORD will speak; for He will surely speak peace to His people and His saints; He will not let them return to folly."

- **The turning point:** After seven verses of petition, the psalmist now pauses to listen. Guzik: "The proper attitude of the believer praying for revival is to surrender to the authority of God's word." Constable: "As the psalmist waited for God to respond, he was confident the Lord would send peace (Heb. shalom, the fullness of divine blessing)."
- **"He will speak peace":** Ellicott says this word "peace" comprehends all that the nation sighed for; to Christians it has a higher meaning still — which is why the Anglican tradition chose this psalm for Christmas Day.
- **"But let them not turn again to folly":** "Folly" here most likely means idolatry (Ellicott), or more broadly a return to sin after mercy received (Gill, Spurgeon). Spurgeon: "To turn again to folly is worse than being foolish for once; it argues wilfulness and obstinacy, and it involves the soul in sevenfold sin." Gill also suggests it may refer to self-righteousness — "the great folly of the Jews to this day."
- **Reformed emphasis (Desiring God):** "Revival begins with God — through his speaking, his voice, his word … When God sends the fire of his Spirit to fall on the hearts of his people … the fire falls on the wood of his word." — https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/revival-in-the-making (search excerpt)

- Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-85/
- Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/85.htm
- Spurgeon: https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps085.php
- Gill: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/85.htm
- Constable: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/psalms-85.html

---

### v. 9 — "Surely His salvation is near to those who fear Him, that His glory may dwell in our land."

- **"Salvation is near":** Gill reads this as a reference to the nearness of Christ's first coming — "the coming of the Saviour was at hand … in a little time." It is near "to those who fear Him" — not to the wicked, from whom salvation is far (Psalm 119:155).
- **"Glory may dwell in our land":** Gill says "glory" here is Christ Himself — "who is the brightness of his Father's glory … who, when he was incarnate, dwelt among men, particularly in the land of Judea." Ellicott ties it to the return of the ark as symbol of God's presence. Constable: "The idea behind glory dwelling in the land is that God would again manifest His presence there by blessing the Israelites."
- Spurgeon: "Israel was glorious whenever she was faithful — her dishonour always followed her disloyalty."

- Gill: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/85.htm
- Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/85.htm
- Constable: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/psalms-85.html
- Spurgeon: https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps085.php

---

### v. 10 — "Loving devotion and faithfulness have joined together; righteousness and peace have kissed."

- **The great reconciliation of divine attributes:** This is the theological high point of the psalm. In human experience, mercy and truth seem opposed — mercy wants to pardon, truth demands condemnation. In God's salvation, they "meet together" (Ellicott: the Hebrew word is used of those who should be friends but whom circumstances have sundered, Proverbs 22:2).
- **Christological fulfilment:** All the older commentators see this fulfilled in the cross. Gill explains: God's essential justice will not admit pardon without satisfaction; Christ was set forth as propitiation so that God might be "just, and appear to be so, when he is the justifier of him that believes in Jesus." Spurgeon: "In him, the attributes of God unite in glad unanimity in the salvation of guilty men … God is as true as if he had fulfilled every letter of his threatenings, as righteous as if he had never spoken peace to a sinner's conscience."
- **Reformed emphasis (Ligonier):** "Our Father graciously restores peace between Himself and us in Christ Jesus. This peace is permanent, for it is not based on ignoring our sins and faults but on God's sure willingness to accept the perfect payment of Jesus in our behalf." — https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/redemptions-drama (search excerpt)
- **Methodist (Whedon):** "'Mercy' and 'peace' can never be granted but upon the grounds of 'truth' and 'righteousness.' Men must abjure all sin, and aim to fulfil all righteousness by a holy [life]." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/psalms-85.html (search excerpt)

- Gill: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/85.htm
- Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/85.htm
- Spurgeon: https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps085.php
- Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-85/

---

### v. 11 — "Faithfulness sprouts from the earth, and righteousness looks down from heaven."

- **Earth and heaven in harmony:** Ellicott explains that "truth" (faithfulness) springs from the earth because the renewal of fertility (rain, harvest) has re-established confidence in God's faithfulness. "Righteousness" looks down "as from a window or battlement" (Song of Solomon 6:10) — it had been hidden like the sun behind a cloud but now shows its benign face. Constable sees lovingkindness and righteousness as what God provides; truth and peace as what His people experience.
- **Christological (Gill):** "Truth" here may be Christ Himself — "who is the way, the truth, and the life" — springing from the earth in His incarnation (cf. Psalm 85:11 with Psalm 139:15, "curiously wrought in the lowest parts of the earth"). "Righteousness" is God the Father looking down from heaven with pleasure on Christ's obedience and sacrifice.
- Spurgeon: "Earth yielding flowers of truth, and heaven shining with stars of holiness; the spheres echoing to each other … Earth carpeted with truth and canopied with righteousness, shall be a nether heaven."

- Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/85.htm
- Gill: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/85.htm
- Spurgeon: https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps085.php
- Constable: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/psalms-85.html

---

### v. 12 — "The LORD will indeed provide what is good, and our land will yield its increase."

- **Material and spiritual blessing together:** Ellicott stresses that "nothing is more instructive than the blending in vv. 12–13 of material and moral blessings. They do go together, as experience, especially national, testifies." The curse of barrenness flees with the curse of sin. Spurgeon: "When the people yielded what was due to God, the soil would recompense their husbandry."
- **"Our land will yield her increase":** Constable ties this to the Mosaic covenant blessings (Deuteronomy 28:1–14) — productive harvests were promised for obedience. Gill extends the metaphor spiritually: believers "increase with the increase of God, bring forth fruits of righteousness."
- Ellicott notes the cry of the psalm likely arose from dread of famine, which was always regarded as judgment for national sin.

- Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/85.htm
- Spurgeon: https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps085.php
- Gill: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/85.htm
- Constable: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/psalms-85.html

---

### v. 13 — "Righteousness will go before Him to prepare the way for His steps."

- **"Righteousness shall go before Him":** Guzik: "Righteousness so marks God that it goes before Him, as the tail of a comet goes behind the comet." God's righteousness is His herald and forerunner.
- **"And shall make His footsteps our pathway" (BSB: "to prepare the way for His steps"):** Ellicott renders: "Righteousness shall walk in front of Him, and follow in His steps" — a better translation of the Hebrew, suggesting righteousness both precedes and follows God. Gill sees John the Baptist as this "righteousness" going before Christ: "John the Baptist … was the forerunner and harbinger of Christ, went before him, and prepared the way for him" (Luke 1:76). Spurgeon: "God's march of right will leave a track wherein his people will joyfully follow."
- **Eschatological hope:** Guzik notes this points forward to the completion at the end of the age, when creation itself is delivered (Romans 8:21). Spurgeon closes: "Such are the blessings of our Lord's first advent, and such shall be yet more conspicuously the result of his second coming. Even so, come Lord Jesus."

- Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-85/
- Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/85.htm
- Gill: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/85.htm
- Spurgeon: https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps085.php

## Tradition-Specific Readings

### Where Protestant traditions differ

The differences on Psalm 85 are more of emphasis than outright disagreement. All traditions see it as a prayer for revival and a Messianic psalm fulfilled in Christ. However:

- **Reformed (Ligonier, Desiring God):** Heavy emphasis on v. 10 as depicting the atonement — the cross as the place where God's justice and mercy meet, with Christ bearing the legal penalty. Revival comes *through the Word preached*, not through emotional experience alone. — https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/redemptions-drama ; https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/revival-in-the-making

- **Baptist (Spurgeon, Gill, Garner-Howes):** Emphasise personal conversion, individual faith, and the perseverance of the saints. Gill reads v. 8's "turn again to folly" as a warning against self-righteousness and rejecting Christ. Spurgeon stresses that revival is God's sovereign work yet something we must pray for. Garner-Howes reads v. 4's Hebrew as expressing faith so strong it speaks of the answer as already accomplished. — https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps085.php ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/85.htm

- **Methodist/Wesleyan (Whedon):** Emphasises the need for human cooperation with divine grace. Whedon on vv. 10–11: "Men must abjure all sin, and aim to fulfil all righteousness by a holy [life]" — grace is never granted apart from truth and righteousness. The "turn us" of v. 4 implies both divine enablement and human response. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/psalms-85.html (search excerpt)

- **Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word / David Guzik):** Emphasises revival as a present, experienceable work of the Spirit, and prayer for revival as something every believer should practice "with bold humility and expectation." Guzik specifically applies v. 6 to praying for pastors, congregations, and communities. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-85/

- **Anglican (Ellicott):** Notes that the psalm was appointed for Christmas Day in the Anglican lectionary — the "peace" of v. 8, the "glory dwelling in our land" of v. 9, and the reconciliation of attributes in v. 10 all pointing to the Incarnation. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/85.htm

### Other views

- **Catholic and Orthodox:** No direct pages from newadvent.org, catholic.com, or oca.org were retrieved in the available searches. Ellicott's and Gill's commentaries (both pre-modern and widely used across traditions) provide readings compatible with Catholic and Orthodox interpretation — especially the strong Christological and incarnational reading of vv. 9–11.

- **Modern scholarship:** Not retrieved due to search/fetch limits (bibleodyssey.org, netbible.org were not reached). Constable (Dallas Theological Seminary) represents a moderate evangelical scholarly approach, situating the psalm as a national lament possibly from the post-exilic period and noting the genre and covenant background.

- **Prosperity / Word of Faith / Hyper-grace:** No direct sources from those movements were retrieved. The traditional commentators uniformly reject any reading that would separate material blessing (v. 12) from moral obedience — Ellicott explicitly says material and moral blessings "do go together" in national experience, and Spurgeon ties the land's yield to the people yielding "what was due to God." These would stand as correctives to any teaching that claims the land's increase apart from repentance and the fear of the Lord.
